analysis.investment_thesis: Can Fin Homes is a conservatively run housing finance company with strong net profit growth of 22% CAGR (3Y) and a cheap valuation at 11.9x P/E, benefiting from India's structural housing demand. However, the business is inherently leveraged (D/E 6.59), finance costs are growing at 29% — faster than revenue at 19% — signalling NIM compression ahead.
key_strengths: Net profit CAGR of 22.1% over three years meets my earnings growth threshold; loan book growing steadily from INR 24,189 Cr (FY22) to INR 34,898 Cr (FY25)
Affordable housing focus serves first-time homebuyers with strong government policy tailwinds (PMAY, interest subsidies) and large unmet demand
Attractive valuation: P/E of 11.9x and P/B of 2.12x are low for a quality HFC with consistent profitability
key_risks: Finance costs growing at 29.3% CAGR vs. revenue at 18.8% — cost of funds rising faster than yields, which will erode spreads if rates stay elevated
D/E of 6.59 is unavoidable for an HFC but means any asset quality deterioration (NPA spike) or credit market disruption has amplified consequences
Promoter stake of only 29.99% (Canara Bank) and possible government ownership influence can limit strategic agility and management ambition
red_flags: OCF was negative in FY22 (INR -3,916 Cr) and FY23 (INR -4,044 Cr) — while structurally normal for a growing lender, it highlights capital dependency
Absence of EBITDA/operating income data for the full history makes trend analysis incomplete; margin visibility is limited
analysis.detailed_analysis:
Financial services companies are not my natural habitat — I prefer businesses where innovation and product development create compounding advantages. Can Fin Homes is a well-run lender, not a disruptive financial platform. The profit growth is real and the housing tailwind is powerful, but the core engine is spread management on a leverage stack, which is fundamentally different from the scalable, margin-expanding businesses I seek. Management appears competent within the HFC model but there is no evidence of the kind of visionary, long-horizon thinking I associate with my best investments.

The valuation is genuinely cheap at 11.9x P/E, which creates a floor. Current holders should maintain positions as India's housing cycle has room to run, but I would not be building a large position here — it lacks the innovation moat and management dynamism that justify concentration.
